text: Everything so far has been about scoping what a grant covers. This lesson is about something different: how a principal proves who it is in the first place, and why that choice matters almost as much as the permissions themselves. IAM users and IAM roles can end up with identical permissions policies and still carry very different risk, purely because of how each one authenticates.

An IAM user holds credentials that exist until someone rotates or deletes them — a console password, and optionally one or more access keys. Those are valid indefinitely by default. An IAM role has no credentials of its own at all. Anyone permitted to use it calls sts:AssumeRole and gets back temporary security credentials — an access key, secret key, and session token, with an expiration measured in minutes to hours. If a leak happens, the exposure window is whatever's left of that session, not forever.

A role actually runs on two separate policies. The trust policy, attached to the role, answers only one question: who is allowed to assume it. Here, it's the EC2 service itself, which is how instance profiles work. The permissions policy is the ordinary IAM policy that answers the second question: once assumed, what can this role actually do. You can grant one without the other, and conflating them is a common source of confusion.

The classic mistake is creating an IAM user and embedding its access key into an application's config. That key ends up on disk, in deployment artifacts, maybe in version control history. The fix is an instance profile, a Lambda execution role, or an ECS task role — the compute service assumes the role for the workload, and the SDK picks up auto-rotating temporary credentials automatically. Nothing long-lived to leak in the first place.

The same logic applies to people. AWS's current recommendation is IAM Identity Center, federating your workforce identity provider into temporary, role-based access across every account in your Organization instead of standing IAM users. When a long-lived key really is unavoidable, rotate it on a schedule, scope it tightly, and pull the IAM credential report periodically — proving when a key was last rotated is a different claim than just saying you rotate keys.

Roles over users, temporary over long-lived — that's the default posture. But even with that posture in place, access can still end up broader than intended through resource policies, cross-account grants, and public exposure. Next lesson covers the tool built specifically to surface that: IAM Access Analyzer.
